pages.title: Beginner level SQL
pages.content:
Welcome to the **Intermediate level** course on SQL.

Below are some of the basic and beginner level queries that we covered in [Learn SQL](https://www.codechef.com/learn/sql).
- Table / db manipulation
 - **CREATE**, **ALTER**, **INSERT**, **DELETE** allow us to create a table or make changes to an existing table
- Queries
 - **SELECT** allows us to view entries in a table
 - **WHERE**, **BETWEEN**, **LIKE**, **AND**, **OR** can be added along with **SELECT** to check which entires meet certain conditions 
- Aggregate functions
 - SQL also allows us to use aggregate functions such as **COUNT**, **MAX / MIN**, **SUM**, **AVG** to view aggregate information of the table
 - **GROUP BY** statement in SQL are used to combine rows with identical values into summary rows.\
GROUP BY is frequently used with the syntax **HAVING** to apply filters at a group level

Lets proceed and learn some new **Intermediate level** concepts!

practiceProblems.title: Combining tables with SQL
practiceProblems.description:
In the previous problem our task was to find name of David Lee's Mathematics professor. 
- We were able to do that manually because the number of tables and data in them were few. 
- Combining tables manually takes a lot of effort and is not practical.

In SQL, we use the concept of **JOIN** to achieve this.\
Below is the query to join two tables 'employee' and 'department' in an organisation database.

```sql
 SELECT *
 FROM employee
 JOIN department
 ON employee.employee_id = department.employee_id;
```

The above query does the following
- Joins two tables and outputs a single table. 
- The column 'employee_id' is used to match rows of the tables. i.e. Rows of the tables 'employee' are matched with the rows of the table 'department' which has the same employee_id by applying the condition **employee.employee_id = department.employee_id**.
- Many a times multiple tables will have similar column names, thus to identify a particular column of a table we use the syntax **table_name.column_name**. 

Below mentioned are the tables 'employee' and 'department' 

Table employee: 


| **employee_id** | **employee_Name** | **Desination**
|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|1001|	John Smith|	Sales Manager|
|1002|	Emily Brown|	Operations Executive|	
|1003|	David Lee	|HR Executive	|



Table department: 


|**employee_id**|**department_id** |**department_Name**
|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|1001|SL01|Sales|
|1002|OP01|Operations|
|1003|HR01|Humar Resouce|



The output of the above query is mentioned below:



| **employee_id** | **employee_Name** | **Desination**|**employee_id**|**department_id** |**department_Name**
|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|1001|	John Smith|	Sales Manager|1001|SL01|Sales|
|1002|	Emily Brown|	Operations Executive|1002|OP01|Operations|
|1003|	David Lee	|HR Executive	|1003|HR01|Humar Resouce|

practiceProblems.title: Inner Joins
practiceProblems.description:
In the previous problem our task was to join the table 'student' and 'course'.\
There could be cases where none of the students has opted for a particular course.
- In such cases, when the tables are joined, the rows which does not match are excluded by default. 
- The row which has the name of the course which **IS NOT** opted by any of the student **WILL BE EXCLUDED** when both the tables are joined.

When the tables are joined in this manner its called **Inner Joins**.

Write a query to do the following
- Join the tables 'student' and 'course' and output all its entries.

practiceProblems.title: Left Joins
practiceProblems.description:
We've learned that by default SQL removes the rows which doesn't match while joining tables.

However, if we wish to join two tables whose rows doesn't match, we can do that using **LEFT JOIN**.\
When two tables are joined using 'LEFT JOIN', and if the rows don't match, 
- All the rows in the first table(left) will be kept as such and 
- Whenever a row doesn't a corresponding row in the second table (right), those columns will be kept blank.

Below is the query to join the table 'customer' and 'order' using LEFT JOIN
```sql
 SELECT *
 FROM customer
 LEFT JOIN order
 ON customer.cust_id = order.cust_id;
```

practiceProblems.title: Right Joins
practiceProblems.description:
We've seen how `LEFT JOIN` keeps all rows from the left table, filling in `NULL`s where there's no match in the right table. `RIGHT JOIN` does the opposite.

A **RIGHT JOIN** keeps all rows from the *right* table (the second table listed in the `JOIN` clause) and includes matching rows from the *left* table (the first table listed). 

If a row in the right table doesn't have a corresponding match in the left table:

- All columns from the right table will be included.
- Columns from the left table will be filled with `NULL` values.

Essentially, `RIGHT JOIN` ensures every row from the second (right) table appears in the result, regardless of whether a match exists in the first (left) table.

Here's the general structure:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM customer
RIGHT JOIN order
ON customer.cust_id = order.cust_id;
```

practiceProblems.title: Full Outer Joins
practiceProblems.description:
Now that we've explored `LEFT JOIN` and `RIGHT JOIN`, let's look at a join that combines both: the **FULL OUTER JOIN**. A `FULL OUTER JOIN` (sometimes just called `FULL JOIN`) returns *all* rows from *both* tables.

Here's a breakdown of how `FULL OUTER JOIN` works:

* **Matching Rows:** If a row in one table has a matching row in the other table (based on the `ON` clause), the join combines those rows into a single row in the result.
* **Unmatched Rows in Left Table:** If a row in the *left* table does *not* have a match in the *right* table, the join includes that row. The columns from the right table will be filled with `NULL` values.
* **Unmatched Rows in Right Table:** If a row in the *right* table does *not* have a match in the *left* table, the join *also* includes that row. The columns from the left table will be filled with `NULL` values.

In short, a `FULL OUTER JOIN` guarantees that every row from *both* tables appears in the result set, with `NULL`s used to fill in missing values where there's no match. It's a combination of `LEFT JOIN` and `RIGHT JOIN`. It doesn't omit any rows from the tables that are being joined.

Here's the general syntax:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM table1
FULL OUTER JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;
```

 - FULL OUTER JOIN the `student` and `course` tables using *'Course_id'* to match the tables. Output the joined table.

* **Unmatched Rows in Right Table:** If a row in the *right* table does *not* have a match in the *left* table, the join *also* includes that row. The columns from the left table will be filled with `NULL` values.

In short, a `FULL OUTER JOIN` guarantees that every row from *both* tables appears in the result set, with `NULL`s used to fill in missing values where there's no match. It's a combination of `LEFT JOIN` and `RIGHT JOIN`. It doesn't omit any rows from the tables that are being joined.

Here's the general syntax:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM table1
FULL OUTER JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;
```

practiceProblems.title: Self Joins
practiceProblems.description:
Sometimes, you need to join a table to *itself*. This is called a **self join**. It's not a distinct type of `JOIN` like `INNER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, or `FULL`; rather, it's a technique where you use any of those join types, but the left and right tables are the *same* table. You treat the table as if it were two separate tables, typically using aliases to distinguish them.

Self joins are crucial when you need to compare rows within the same table or when you have hierarchical data within a single table. Think of situations like:

* **Employee-Manager Relationships:** A single `employees` table might have an `employee_id` column and a `manager_id` column (which also references `employee_id`). To find each employee's manager, you'd join the table to itself.
* **Finding Pairs:** You might want to find pairs of employees who live in the same city.
* **Parts List** Consider a scenario in mechanical industry where a self-join helps retrieve hierarchical relationships in a Bill of Materials (BOM) by linking components to their parent assemblies within the same table.

Here's the general idea, using aliases (`a` and `b` in this case):

```sql
SELECT
 e1.employee_name AS Employee,
 e2.employee_name AS Manager
FROM
 employees AS e1 -- Alias for employee
INNER JOIN
 employees AS e2 -- Alias for manager
ON
 e1.manager_id = e2.employee_id;
```

### Key Points:

1.**Table Aliases:** You must use table aliases (like a and b above) to differentiate between the "two" instances of the same table. Without aliases, the database wouldn't know which instance you're referring to.

2.**Join Condition:** The ON clause is critical. It defines how rows within the same table are related. This is where you specify the relationship you're investigating (e.g., a.manager_id = b.employee_id). The Join Condition cannot have same name on both sides of comparison, that will include all the entries in the table.

3.**Join Types:** Although its mostly used with the INNER JOIN, any of the previously dicussed joins could also be used in SELF JOIN.

practiceProblems.title: Cross join
practiceProblems.description:
In the past few problems we've learned how to join the tables which were inter related. \
Now, lets try to join tables which are not at all related.\
We use the concept of **CROSS JOIN** to join such tables. Below is query to cross join the tables 'Manufacture' and 'Model'
 ```sql
 SELECT *
 FROM Manufacture
 CROSS JOIN Model
```

Below mentioned are the tables 'Manufacture' and 'Model'

Table Manufacture: 


| **mfg_id** | **company** 
|:----:|:-----:|
|1001|	Hyundai|
|1002|	Tata|
|1003|	Suzuki|



Table Model: 


| **cmp_id** | **company** 
|:----:|:-----:|
|1|Sedan|
|2|Suv|

|1002|	Tata|2|Suv|

pages.title: Primary Key vs Foreign Key
pages.content:
Primary Key in a table is used to uniquely identify a row in a table. It also has a certain criteria 
- The value should not be NULL
- Each value should be unique
- A table should not have more than one Primary key

You might have already observed that primary keys are used to join tables.\
Joining the table is only possible if there is a matching column in the tables which are to be joined.\
Which means that a table's primary key can be found in a different table.

A primary key of a table when present in a different table is referred to as a **Foreign Key**.\
In the below table student, St_id is a **Primary key** and Course_id (which is a primary key of the table 'course') is a **Foreign Key**

Table student: 


| **St_id** | **St_Name** | **Department** | **Course_id** 
|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|1001|	John Smith|	Computer Science|	CS101|
|1002|	Emily Brown|	History|	HIS102|
|1003|	David Lee	|Mathematics	|MAT202|



Table course: 


|**Course_id** |**Course_Name**|**Credits**|**Prof_id** 
|:----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|CS101|Introduction to Computer Science|3|2001|
|HIS102|World History II	|3|2004|
|MAT202|Linear Algebra|2|2002|




Below is the query to create a table student defining St_id as the Primary Key and Course_id(from the table 'course') as foreign key.
 ```sql
 CREATE TABLE student (
 St_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 St_Name TEXT,
 Department TEXT,
 Course_id TEXT,
 FOREIGN KEY (Course_id) REFERENCES course(Course_id)
 );
```

pages.title: Composite, Candidate, Alternate, and Super Keys
pages.content:
Database keys are essential for uniquely identifying records within a table and for establishing relationships between tables. Let's explore composite, candidate, alternate, and super keys using a single `Products` table as an example.

**Table: `Products`**

| product_id | product_code | product_name | product_model | price | manufacturer |
|------------|--------------|-----------------|---------------|-------|--------------|
| 1 | ABC123 | Widget A | Model X | 10.00 | Acme Corp |
| 2 | XYZ456 | Gadget B | Model Y | 20.00 | Beta Inc |
| 3 | PQR789 | Widget A | Model Z | 15.00 | Acme Corp |
| 4 | ABC124 | Widget A | Model X | 11.00 | Gamma Ltd |
| 5 | LMN001 | Thingamajig C | Model Alpha | 25.00 | Acme Corp |

**Composite Key:**

* **Definition:** A combination of two or more columns that uniquely identifies a row when a single column is not sufficient.
* **Example:** In the `Products` table, let's assume that while `product_id` alone is usually unique, sometimes we track similar products across different manufacturers. Thus it is recommended to combine more data from other keys!
 * The combination of `product_name` and `manufacturer` *might* uniquely identify products, assuming no two manufacturers produce the *exact* same named product. However, in the current listing, duplicates of `product_name` and `manufacturer` exist, thus it is less suited to becoming a Composite Key.

**Candidate Key:**

* **Definition:** A column or set of columns that can *uniquely* identify a row in a table. A table can have multiple candidate keys.
* **Example:**
 * `product_id` is a candidate key. It's designed to be unique for each product.
 * `product_code` is also a candidate key, assuming that it is assigned and tracked uniquely to provide records across the data. We can add to product with the attribute for being uniquely candidate.

**Alternate Key:**

* **Definition:** A candidate key that is *not* chosen as the primary key. It's a uniquely identifying column/set that could have been the primary key.
* **Example:**
 * If we choose `product_id` as the primary key, then `product_code` becomes an alternate key.

* **SQL:** `CREATE TABLE` statement

 ```sql
 CREATE TABLE Products (
 product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, -- Designated as the primary key
 product_code VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE, -- An alternate key: made unique
 product_name VARCHAR(255),
 product_model VARCHAR(255),
 price DECIMAL(10, 2),
 manufacturer VARCHAR(255)
 );
 ```

**Super Key:**

* **Definition:** A set of one or more attributes (columns) that uniquely identifies a row in a table. It is a superset of the candidate key(s), meaning any set of columns containing a candidate key qualifies as a super key. Unlike candidate keys, a super key does not have to be minimal—it can include additional attributes that are not strictly necessary for uniqueness.
In the statements above, unique keys have been proven to identify rows using a super key. However, a super key can also contain multiple sets of attributes, as long as it ensures row 


* **Example:**
 * `{product_id}` is a super key (it contains the candidate key `product_id`).
 * `{product_id, product_name}` is also a super key. The extra column (`product_name`) is not *required* to uniquely identify the record, but its presence doesn't invalidate the super key property. Because if we were not getting 4 key options it's best pick will be used at most scenarios from its given database.

**SQL (Creating the table demonstrating keys):**

```sql
CREATE TABLE Products (
 product_id INT PRIMARY KEY, -- Candidate Key, and Primary Key
 product_code VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE, -- Candidate Key, and Alternate Key
 product_name VARCHAR(255),
 product_model VARCHAR(255),
 price DECIMAL(10, 2),
 manufacturer VARCHAR(255)
);
```

practiceProblems.title: Foreign Key and Unique Key
practiceProblems.description:
A `foreign key` is a column (or set of columns) in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. Foreign keys are used to enforce referential integrity in a relational database, ensuring that relationships between tables are consistent. They are used to link two tables together. 
A `unique key` on a table enforces that a column or a combination of columns is unique across all the rows of the table. This allows us to implement important rules related to database records.

**Example:**

Let's consider two tables: `Customers` and `Orders`. We will use unique keys for emails to ensure that each email is accepted only once, preventing duplication. 

**Table: `Customers`**

| customer_id | customer_name | city | customer_email |
|-------------|---------------|-----------|-----------------------|
| 1 | John Doe | New York | john.doe@example.com |
| 2 | Jane Smith | London | jane.smith@example.com |
| 3 | David Lee | Paris | david.lee@example.com |

**Table: `Orders`**

| order_id | customer_id | order_date | amount |
|----------|-------------|------------|--------|
| 101 | 1 | 2023-01-15 | 100 |
| 102 | 2 | 2023-02-20 | 250 |
| 103 | 1 | 2023-03-10 | 50 |
| 104 | 4 | 2023-04-05 | 120 |

In this example:

* `customer_id` in the `Customers` table is the primary key.
* `customer_email` in the `Customers` table has a unique property, so any future records or edits that duplicate other emails will not pass.
* `customer_id` in the `Orders` table is a foreign key referencing the `Customers` table.

**SQL (Creating the tables with foreign key and unique key constraint):**
```sql
CREATE TABLE parent_table (
 parent_column_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 parent_column1 VARCHAR(255),
 parent_column2 VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE, -- Unique constraint on a single column
 parent_column3 INT,
 UNIQUE (parent_column1, parent_column3) -- Composite Unique constraint
);

CREATE TABLE child_table (
 child_column_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 child_column1 VARCHAR(255),
 parent_column_id INT,
 FOREIGN KEY (parent_column_id) REFERENCES parent_table(parent_column_id) -- Foreign key constraint
);
```
### Task
* Write the SQL query to create the tables given above (`Customers` & `Orders`) with the given constraints like primary key, unique key, foreign key (do not insert data into the table).

**Explanation:**

* The `FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)` clause in the `Orders` table specifies that the `customer_id` column is a foreign key.
* `REFERENCES Customers(customer_id)` indicates that this foreign key references the `customer_id` column in the `Customers` table.
* The `UNIQUE` constraint on the `customer_email` column in the `Customers` table ensures that each email address is unique, preventing duplicate entries.

**What the Foreign Key Constraint Enforces:**

* An order cannot be created for a `customer_id` that does not exist in the `Customers` table. This ensures that orders are always associated with valid customers. If customer 4 doesn't exist in the `Customers` table, it will not be possible to add the value to the `Orders` table with `customer_id` 4.
* The unique constraint on the email column will not allow duplicate emails to be entered into the customers table.

practiceProblems.title: ON DELETE CASCADE & ON UPDATE CASCADE
practiceProblems.description:
Cascading, in the context of foreign key constraints, refers to the automatic propagation of changes (specifically deletions and updates) from a parent table to its related child tables. This ensures data integrity by maintaining consistency between related tables.

Here's a breakdown of how cascading works with `ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE` including tables and examples:

* **Concept:**
 * `ON DELETE CASCADE`: When a row is deleted from the *parent* table, all corresponding rows in the *child* table that have a foreign key referencing the deleted parent row are automatically deleted.
 * `ON UPDATE CASCADE`: When the primary key value of a row is updated in the *parent* table, the corresponding foreign key values in the *child* table are automatically updated to match.
 * This is useful when the existence of child rows is entirely dependent on the existence of the parent row, and when parent primary key changes must propagate to child records.
 * It ensures that there are no "orphan" records in the child table (records that refer to a non-existent or outdated parent).

* **Example:**

 * **Parent Table: `Customers`**

 | customer_id | customer_name | city |
 |-------------|---------------|----------|
 | 1 | John Doe | New York |
 | 2 | Jane Smith | London |
 | 3 | David Lee | Paris |

 * **Child Table: `Orders`**

 | order_id | customer_id | order_date | amount |
 |----------|-------------|------------|--------|
 | 101 | 1 | 2023-01-15 | 100 |
 | 102 | 2 | 2023-02-20 | 250 |
 | 103 | 1 | 2023-03-10 | 50 |

 * **SQL (Creating the tables with ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE):**

 ```sql
 CREATE TABLE Customers (
 customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 customer_name VARCHAR(255),
 city VARCHAR(255)
 );

 CREATE TABLE Orders (
 order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 customer_id INT,
 order_date DATE,
 amount DECIMAL(10, 2),
 FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
 );
 ```

 * **Behavior:**
 * If you delete `customer_id = 1` from `Customers`, orders 101 and 103 will also be deleted from `Orders`.
 * If you update `customer_id` from 1 to 4 in Customers, the customer_id in orders 101 and 103 will also be updated to 4.

### Task
* Write a DELETE query to delete John Doe's details from `Customers` table and see changes in `Orders` table.

**Key points:**
* It maintains strict referential integrity by automatically removing or updating dependent data.
* Use it when you want to ensure that related child rows are always removed or updated when the parent row is deleted or updated.

### **In Summary:**
- **`ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE`** removes or updates child rows.
- Cascading actions help maintain data integrity and consistency in relational databases. They automate the process of handling related data when parent rows are deleted or updated.

practiceProblems.title: ON DELETE SET NULL & ON UPDATE SET NULL
practiceProblems.description:
- **`ON DELETE SET NULL`**: When a row is deleted from the *parent* table, the foreign key column(s) in the related rows of the *child* table are set to `NULL`. 
- **`ON UPDATE SET NULL`**: When the primary key value of a row is updated in the *parent* table, the corresponding foreign key values in the *child* table are set to `NULL`. 
- This is useful when the child rows can still exist independently of the parent row, but the relationship is no longer valid. 
- It allows you to preserve the child data while indicating that the relationship has been broken. 
- It is critical that the foreign key column allows `NULL` values. 

## Example 

### **Parent Table: `Customers`** 

| customer_id | customer_name | city |
|------------|---------------|----------|
| 1 | John Doe | New York |
| 2 | Jane Smith | London |
| 3 | David Lee | Paris |

### **Child Table: `Orders`** 

| order_id | customer_id | order_date | amount |
|----------|------------|------------|--------|
| 101 | 1 | 2023-01-15 | 100 |
| 102 | 2 | 2023-02-20 | 250 |
| 103 | 1 | 2023-03-10 | 50 |

### **SQL (Creating the tables with `ON DELETE/UPDATE SET NULL`)** 

```sql
CREATE TABLE Customers (
 customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 customer_name VARCHAR(255),
 city VARCHAR(255)
);

CREATE TABLE Orders (
 order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 customer_id INT NULL, -- customer_id can be NULL
 order_date DATE,
 amount DECIMAL(10, 2),
 FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customers(customer_id) 
 ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE SET NULL
);
```
### **Behavior:**
- If you delete `customer_id = 1` from `Customers`, `customer_id` in orders `101` and `103` will be set to `NULL`. 
- If you update `customer_id` from `1` to `4` in `Customers`, the `customer_id` in orders `101` and `103` will be set to `NULL`. 

### Task
* Write a delete query to delete John Doe's details from `Customers` table and notice the changes in the `Orders` table

### **Key Points:**
- It maintains referential integrity by preventing orphaned records. 
- It allows you to preserve child data while indicating a broken relationship. 
- Use it when child rows can exist independently of the parent row, but the relationship is optional. 

### **In Summary:**
- **`ON DELETE/UPDATE SET NULL`** sets the Foreign Key column to `NULL` in the child rows.

practiceProblems.title: Union
practiceProblems.description:
Till now, we have joined tables by columns. Now let’s join the data by rows.\
We use the concept of **UNION** to do that.\
UNION helps us to place a table right on top of another table.\
There are set of criteria to be followed while appending the tables:
 - The number of columns of the tables should be same.
 - The data type of the table should be of the same order of that of the first table.

Below is query to combine tables 'Mfg_Ind' and 'Mfg_Int'
 ```sql
 SELECT *
 FROM Mfg_Ind
 UNION
 SELECT *
 FROM Mfg_Int;
```

Below mentioned are the tables 'Mfg_Ind' and 'Mfg_Int'

Table Mfg_Ind: 


| **mfg_id** | **company** 
|:----:|:-----:|
|1001|	Mahindra|
|1002|	Tata|



Table Mfg_Int: 


| **Id** | **cmp_name** 
|:----:|:-----:|
|5|Hyundai|
|6|Suzuki|



After executing the above query we get the below mentioned table:


| **mfg_id** | **company** 
|:----:|:-----:|
|1001|	Mahindra|
|1002|	Tata|
|5|Hyundai|
|6|Suzuki|



### Task
Write a query using union to stack the table 'Arts' over 'Science' and output the final table 


### Note:
The UNION statmente removes the duplicate data in the new table formed.

practiceProblems.title: WITH
practiceProblems.description:
**WITH** is used to create temporary tables when we need to define a named subquery that can be referenced later in the SQL statement.
- The same task could have been done by a **WHERE** clause inside a JOIN statement - however, using a **WITH** allows us to reduce the complexity of the query

Let us consider the data base of an organisation, where we have a table 'employee' and a table 'department'.\
Lets find out the department of the top 3 highly paid employees.\
Note that the department details are not mentioned in the table 'employee'.

Below is query to find out the department of the top 3 highly paid employees
 ```sql
 WITH top_employee AS( -- This table has only 2 columns - 'name' and 'emp_id'
 SELECT name,emp_id
 FROM employee
 ORDER BY salary DESC
 LIMIT 3 -- This table has only 3 rows - highest paid employees
 )
 SELECT top_employee.name,department.dept_name
 FROM top_employee
 JOIN department
 ON top_employee.emp_id=department.emp_id;
```

### Task
Rearrange the query to find the name and department of the students who has scored a total marks more than 80.
Table student has the following columns: st_id, st_name, marks,dept_id.
Table department has the following columns:dept_id, dept_name

pages.content:
### One-to-One Relationship (1:1)

- Each record in the first table matches exactly one record in the second table, and vice versa 

**Think of it like this:**

- Like a person and their passport - each person has exactly one passport, and each passport belongs to exactly one person! 



### One-to-One Representation in ERD



### One-to-Many Relationship (1:N)

- One record in the first table can relate to multiple records in the second table, but each record in the second table relates to only one record in the first table 

**Think of it like this:**

- Like a teacher and their students - one teacher can have many students, but each student has only one teacher (in this example)! 



### One-to-Many Representation in ERD



### Many-to-Many Relationship (M:N)

- Multiple records in the first table can relate to multiple records in the second table 

**Think of it like this:**

- Like students and courses - a student can take multiple courses, and each course can have multiple students! 



### Many-to-Many Representation in ERD

pages.title: Attributes - further types
pages.content:
### Multi-valued Attribute

- A multi-valued attribute is when a single attribute can hold multiple values. It's like having multiple answers to the same question.

**Think of it like this:**

- You know how some people have multiple phone numbers? Like one for work, one personal, and maybe one home number? That's a multi-valued attribute - one person can have several phone numbers, and they're all valid!



(Note: In real relational databases, we'd typically create a separate table for phone numbers to handle this better)

**Multi-valued Attribute Representation in ERD:**

- Multivalued attribute is represented by a double oval.



**Points to Remember:**

- Not great for relational databases (we usually split them into separate tables)
- Can make searching and updating complicated
- Better handled through proper normalization
- Common in NoSQL databases

### Derived Attribute

- A derived attribute is something we can calculate from other attributes - we don't need to store it because we can figure it out when needed.

**Think of it like this:**

- It's like your age - if we know your birth date, we don't need to store your age because we can calculate it anytime. The birth date is stored, but age is derived from it.



**Derived Attribute Representation in ERD:**

- Derived attribute is represented by a dashed oval.



**Points to Remember:**

- Not physically stored in the database
- Calculated when needed
- Saves storage space
- Needs to be clearly documented so everyone knows how it's calculated
- Can impact performance if the calculation is complex

pages.title: Functional Dependency
pages.content:
When one piece of data always tells you exactly what another piece of data will be - that's a functional dependency! If A → B, whenever we know A, we'll always know B.

### Think of it like this:

Like your student ID card - if someone knows your student ID number, they can always know your full name. Your name depends on your ID. But knowing just your name doesn't tell us your ID (many students could have the same name)



Notice how ID 101 and 103 have the same name - this shows why name doesn't determine ID!

There are different types of functional dependencies, we'll learn about them in coming lessons

pages.title: Trivial Dependency
pages.content:
A trivial functional dependency is when a set of attributes determines another set, but the determined set is actually just a subset of the first set.

### Think of it like this:

Imagine having your full name (first name + last name). If you know someone's full name, you definitely know their first name, right? That's trivial - it's obvious because the first name is already part of the full name.



This is trivial because First Name is already included in the left side.

### Key Points to Remember:

- If A → B is trivial, B must be a subset of A
- Trivial dependencies are always true by definition
- They're important for understanding database design rules
- They help us identify which dependencies are actually meaningful

pages.title: Non-Trivial Dependency
pages.content:
A non-trivial functional dependency is when one attribute determines another, but the determined attribute isn't just a subset of what we already know. It's like discovering a hidden connection.

### Think of it like this:

Like a student ID determining a GPA - knowing the ID tells you something completely new (the GPA) that wasn't part of the ID itself.

**Trivial Example**

- {StudentID, Name, Age} → {Name}
- Name is already in the left side

**Non-Trivial Example**

- {StudentID} → {GPA}
- GPA is new information

**Library Database Example**



### Key Points to Remember:

- If A → B is non-trivial, B must NOT be a subset of A
- Non-trivial dependencies reveal actual relationships in your data
- They're crucial for database design and normalization
- They help us understand how different pieces of data relate to each other

pages.title: Multivalued Dependency
pages.content:
A multivalued dependency happens when one attribute determines a set of values, and these values are independent of other attributes. We write this as A ↠ B, meaning "A multidetermines B". Think of it as "one-to-many" relationships where the "many" parts don't affect each other

### Think of it like this:

Imagine an employee in a company. Each employee has various skills (like programming languages they know) and works on different projects. Just because an employee knows Python doesn't mean they must work on the website project, and just because they work on the mobile app doesn't mean they must know Java. Their skills and project assignments are independent of each other



- Employee ID ↠ Skills (Employee E101 knows Python, Java, and SQL)
- Employee ID ↠ Projects (E101 works on Website, Mobile App, and Database projects)

Just because E101 knows Python doesn't mean they must work on any specific project. Their skills and project assignments are independent.

### See how this looks in a database

```sql
CREATE TABLE EmployeeSkills (
EmployeeID VARCHAR(10),
Skill VARCHAR(50),
PRIMARY KEY (EmployeeID, Skill)
);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE EmployeeProjects (
EmployeeID VARCHAR(10),
Project VARCHAR(50),
PRIMARY KEY (EmployeeID, Project)
);
```

### Key Points to Remember:

- Multivalued dependencies involve sets of values that are determined by a single attribute
- The determined sets must be independent of each other (like skills and projects)
- We use the double arrow (↠) to show multivalued dependencies
- In databases, we often handle these by creating separate tables for each dependent set
- Understanding these helps in achieving Fourth Normal Form (4NF)

pages.title: Partial Dependency
pages.content:
A partial dependency occurs when a non-key attribute is dependent on only **part** of a composite primary key. A composite key is a primary key made up of two or more attributes. The non-key attribute doesn't need the **entire** primary key to determine its value, just a portion of it.

Think of it like this:

Imagine a table tracking employee training courses. The primary key is a composite of **EmployeeID** and **CourseID**. Now, if **CourseName** is also an attribute in the table, and **CourseName** is determined **only** by **CourseID** (and not the **EmployeeID**), then we have a partial dependency. The employee doesn't affect the course name; the course ID alone is sufficient.

**Example Data (Illustrating Partial Dependency):**

| EmployeeID | CourseID | CourseName | CompletionDate |
|------------|----------|--------------------|----------------|
| 123 | CS101 | Intro to Python | 2023-10-26 |
| 123 | DB201 | Database Design | 2023-11-15 |
| 456 | CS101 | Intro to Python | 2023-11-01 |
| 789 | CS101 | Intro to Python | 2023-11-10 |
| 456 | WEB301 | Advanced Web Dev | 2023-12-01 |

**Let's trace the dependencies:**

* `EmployeeID, CourseID → CompletionDate` (The date an employee completed a specific course.)
* `CourseID → CourseName` (The name of the course based on its ID.)
* Therefore, `EmployeeID, CourseID → CourseName` (Partial Dependency - `CourseName` only depends on `CourseID`, a part of the primary key)

**See how this looks in a database:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE EmployeeTraining (
 EmployeeID VARCHAR(10),
 CourseID VARCHAR(10),
 CourseName VARCHAR(50),
 CompletionDate DATE,
 PRIMARY KEY (EmployeeID, CourseID)
);
```
In this table, `CourseName` is partially dependent on `CourseID` which is part of the primary key (`EmployeeID`, `CourseID`).

**Key Points to Remember:**

* Partial dependencies only apply when you have a composite primary key.
* They lead to redundancy (the same `CourseName` is repeated for every employee who takes the course).
* They cause update anomalies (if you want to change a `CourseName`, you have to update it in multiple rows).
* To remove a partial dependency, create a new table with the attribute(s) that make up the partial dependency, and the attribute(s) that depend on it.

pages.title: Partial Dependency- Practice
pages.content:
Consider the three tables with details as given below.

## **1. Order Processing System** 
In an order processing system: 
- **OrderID** and **ProductID** together determine **Quantity**. 
- **ProductID** determines the standard **ProductPrice**. 
- However, special promotions might change the **ProductPrice** for a specific **OrderID** and **ProductID** combination on a particular day. 

---

## **2. University Enrollment System** 
In a university enrollment system: 
- **StudentID** and **CourseID** together determine **EnrollmentDate**. 
- Each **CourseID** has a fixed number of **CourseCredits** that never changes once the course is created and remains the same for all students enrolled in that course. 

---

## **3. Hotel Reservation System** 
In a hotel reservation system: 
- **BookingID** and **RoomNumber** together determine **CheckInDate**. 
- **RoomNumber** determines the **RoomType**. 
- **RoomType** primarily determines the **RoomPricePerNight**, but the **RoomPricePerNight** is also impacted by **SeasonalDemand**, which applies to all room types for a specific **BookingID** (e.g., holidays).

pages.title: Transitive Dependency
pages.content:
A transitive dependency occurs when there's an indirect relationship between attributes. If A → B and B → C, then A → C is a transitive dependency. It's like a chain reaction where one piece of information leads to another, which leads to yet another

### Think of it like this:

In a supply chain, imagine a manufacturer who works with specific suppliers, and each supplier has their own warehouse location. If you know the manufacturer, you know their supplier, and knowing the supplier tells you the warehouse location. So indirectly, knowing the manufacturer tells you the warehouse location



**Let's trace the dependencies**

- Manufacturer ID → Supplier ID (Each manufacturer works with one supplier)
- Supplier ID → Warehouse Location (Each supplier has one warehouse)
- Therefore, Manufacturer ID → Warehouse Location (Transitive)

### See how this looks in a database

```sql
CREATE TABLE Manufacturers (
ManufacturerID VARCHAR(10),
SupplierID VARCHAR(10),
PRIMARY KEY (ManufacturerID)
);
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE SupplierWarehouse (
SupplierID VARCHAR(10),
WarehouseLocation VARCHAR(50),
PRIMARY KEY (SupplierID)
);
```

### Key Points to Remember:

- Transitive dependencies involve indirect relationships through intermediate attributes
- They can lead to data redundancy and update anomalies if not properly normalized
- Identifying transitive dependencies is crucial for achieving 3NF (Third Normal Form)
- Not all chains of dependencies are transitive - the relationship must exist solely through the chain
- Breaking down transitive dependencies often leads to creating separate tables

pages.title: What is Normalisation
pages.content:
Database normalization is a step-by-step process of organizing your data to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. Think of it as creating a set of rules for your database that helps prevent data inconsistencies and makes updates easier. 

### Think of it like this:

Imagine your messy closet where you throw everything in one drawer. Finding things is hard, and you often have duplicate items! Normalization is like organizing that closet into separate drawers for socks, shirts, and pants - everything has its perfect place! 

- But it goes even further - it's like also creating a catalog system that helps you know:
 - Which clothes belong to which season
 - How different pieces can be matched together
 - When you last wore each item

### Let's say you're managing a school system



**see the repeated data?**

- Normalization is a step-by-step process. There are different normal forms, we'll cover 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF, BCNF, 4NF and 5NF.
- Each step builds on the previous one which means that every normal form has already passed the rules of the previous form. 

### Pro Tips 

- Ask yourself: "Does this data really belong here?" If not, it probably needs its own table.
- Remember: Normalization might mean more tables, but it means less redundant data!
- Sometimes denormalization is okay for performance - but normalize first, then denormalize if needed!

pages.title: First Normal Form (1NF)
pages.content:
1NF is all about making your data atomic - which means breaking down information into its smallest meaningful parts! No more comma-separated lists or multiple values in one cell.

Key Rules of 1NF:

- Each table cell must contain a single value (atomic values)
- Each column must have a unique name
- Values in each column must be of the same type
- Each record must be unique (no duplicate rows)

### Messy school data



**Problems with this table**

- Courses column contains multiple values
- Multiple phone numbers in one cell
- Teacher information is combined and not atomic

### Neat, atomic data



**Improvements after 1NF**

- Each cell now contains a single value (atomic)
- Phone numbers are stored in a separate table, one per row
- Course enrollments are separated, with one course per row
- Each table has a clear purpose and all columns contain the same type of data
- We can easily add or remove phone numbers without affecting other data
- Course enrollments are now clearly linked to both students and teachers

pages.title: Second Normal Form (2NF)
pages.content:
2NF is about making sure non-key attributes depend on the WHOLE primary key, not just part of it! Remember: You need to be in 1NF first!

### Look at Student Enrollments table



**Problems with this table:**

- Course credits (3, 4) are repeated for each student taking the same course
- Teacher department is repeated whenever the same teacher appears
- These partial dependencies cause redundancy and potential inconsistencies




**Improvements after 2NF:**

- Course information (credits) is stored once per course
- Teacher information (department) is stored once per teacher
- Student Enrollments table only contains the relationships
- Updating a course's credits or teacher's department only needs to happen in one place
- No more redundant data about courses or teachers

### How to Achieve 2NF

**Step-by-Step Approach**
- Identify the primary key (single or composite)
- Check each non-key attribute
- Ask: "Does this attribute depend on the WHOLE key?"
- If not, move it to a new table!

pages.title: Third Normal Form (3NF)
pages.content:
3NF eliminates transitive dependencies - when a non-key column depends on another non-key column instead of the primary key.For a table to be in 3NF, it should already be in 2NF.

**Think of it like this:**

It's like a game of telephone - if you need to go through Bob to get a message to Sally, that's inefficient! Similarly, if you need one column to get information about another column, that's a transitive dependency we need to fix!

### Let's Look at our Teachers table



**Problems with this table:**
- Department budget depends on the department, not directly on the teacher
- Department head depends on the department, not the teacher
- These transitive dependencies cause redundancy when multiple teachers are in the same department



**Improvements after 3NF:**

- Department information (budget, head) is stored once per department
- Teacher table only stores the direct relationship to their department
- Updating a department's budget or head only needs to happen in one place
- No more redundant department information when multiple teachers are in the same department

### Key points

- 3NF ensures all non-key columns depend directly on the primary key
- If column B depends on column A, and A isn't a primary key, move B to a new table with A as its primary key
- This eliminates the "domino effect" where changing one value requires multiple updates
- Results in more tables but each table has a clear, single purpose

pages.title: Boyce Codd Form (BCNF)
pages.content:
BCNF is like a stricter 3NF which means for a table to be in BCNF it has to be in 3NF. In BCNF, every determinant (the attributes that determine other attributes) must be a candidate key. No exceptions!

**Think of it like this:**

Imagine a classroom where only class monitors can assign tasks to students. If a regular student starts assigning tasks, that's a BCNF violation - because only authorized people (candidate keys) should determine assignments! 

### Let's Look at our Teachers table



**Problems with this table:**
- professor_id → course_id (professors teach only one course)
- course_id → professor_id (each course has one professor)
- Both could be candidate keys, but office depends only on professor_id
- Violates BCNF because professor_office depends on professor_id, not on all candidate keys



**Improvements after BCNF:**

- Each table has clear functional dependencies on its primary key
- Professor details are stored separately, eliminating redundancy
- Updates to professor office locations only happen in one place
- Both tables satisfy BCNF requirements

### Key points

- BCNF ensures all functional dependencies are on candidate keys
- A candidate key is any attribute(s) that could serve as a primary key
- BCNF is stronger than 3NF and eliminates certain types of redundancy
- Sometimes requires more tables than 3NF but provides better data integrity

pages.title: Fourth Normal Form (4NF)
pages.content:
4NF deals with multi-valued dependencies - when one attribute determines multiple independent values of other attributes

**Think of it like this:**

Imagine a student who can take multiple courses AND can have multiple hobbies. The courses they take aren't related to their hobbies - they're independent facts about the student

### Let's Look at this table



**Problems with this table:**
- Creates a Cartesian product of skills and languages
- Redundant repetition of student name
- Hard to maintain - adding a new language requires multiple rows
- Difficult to understand which combinations are valid



**Improvements after 4NF:**

- Each multi-valued dependency is in its own table
- No redundant combinations
- Easy to add new skills or languages independently
- Clear representation of which skills and languages a student has
- Maintains data integrity and eliminates update anomalies

### Key points

- Always consider whether multi-valued facts are truly related
- Don't be afraid to create separate tables for independent facts
- Remember that joining tables can recreate the original view if needed
- Document your design decisions and dependencies

pages.title: Fifth Normal Form (5NF)
pages.content:
Fifth Normal Form (5NF) ensures that a table cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data. When you join these smaller tables back together, you get exactly the same data—no more, no less!

### Let's see a problematic table



### Why isn't this in 5NF?

- This table satisfies 4NF (no multi-valued dependencies)
- However, it has a cyclic join dependency
- When we split and rejoin the tables, we might get extra rows that weren't in the original data

### Let's see the Join problem

When we decompose and rejoin, look what happens
1. **Split into three tables**



2. **When we join these tables** - We get an extra row that wasn't in our original data



### How to Fix This?

**Create a single table with all three columns as the primary key**



### Why this works:

- The composite key (supplier_id, part_id, project_id) ensures each combination is unique
- No false rows can be generated through joins
- All join dependencies are implied by the candidate key
- The table cannot be decomposed further without losing information

### To achieve 5NF

- Identify all join dependencies
- Check if decomposition is lossless (no spurious tuples when rejoining)
- Verify that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys
- If needed, keep tables combined to prevent data anomalies - Sometimes keeping tables together in 5NF is better than decomposing them

pages.title: Referential Integrity
pages.content:
Referential Integrity is a database concept that ensures relationships between tables remain consistent. It's about maintaining the accuracy and reliability of your data by preventing you from creating "dangling" references.

Think of it like this:

Imagine two tables: `Customers` and `Orders`. The `Orders` table contains a `CustomerID` column that links to the `Customers` table. Referential integrity ensures that you cannot create an order with a `CustomerID` that doesn't exist in the `Customers` table. It also helps prevent deleting a customer if there are existing orders associated with that customer.

### Example Data (Illustrating Referential Integrity):

**Customers Table:**

| CustomerID | FirstName | LastName |
|------------|-----------|----------|
| 1 | John | Doe |
| 2 | Jane | Smith |
| 3 | David | Lee |

**Orders Table:**

| OrderID | CustomerID | OrderDate |
|---------|------------|------------|
| 101 | 1 | 2023-11-20 |
| 102 | 2 | 2023-11-21 |
| 103 | 1 | 2023-11-22 |
| 104 | 4 | 2023-11-23 |

In this example, Order 104 references a `CustomerID` of 4. If there is no Customer with `CustomerID` 4 in the `Customers` table, the database **should** prevent this insertion due to referential integrity.

### Key Terms:

* **Primary Key:** A unique identifier for a record in a table (e.g., `CustomerID` in `Customers` table).
* **Foreign Key:** A column in one table that references the primary key of another table (e.g., `CustomerID` in `Orders` table referencing `Customers.CustomerID`).
* **Parent Table:** The table containing the primary key (e.g., `Customers`).
* **Child Table:** The table containing the foreign key (e.g., `Orders`).

### Database Implementation (SQL):

```sql
CREATE TABLE Customers (
 CustomerID INT PRIMARY KEY,
 FirstName VARCHAR(50),
 LastName VARCHAR(50)
);

CREATE TABLE Orders (
 OrderID INT PRIMARY KEY,
 CustomerID INT,
 OrderDate DATE,
 FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerID)
);
```

In this example, the `FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerID)` clause enforces referential integrity.

**Key Points to Remember:**

* Referential Integrity is enforced through foreign key constraints.
* It prevents you from adding a record to the child table with a foreign key value that doesn't exist in the parent table's primary key.
* It can also control what happens when you try to delete or update a record in the parent table that has related records in the child table.

**Common Referential Integrity Actions:**

* **CASCADE:** If you delete a row in the parent table, related rows in the child table are automatically deleted. If you update a value in the parent table, it updates the value on the child table.
* **SET NULL:** If you delete a row in the parent table, the foreign key values in related rows in the child table are set to `NULL`.
* **SET DEFAULT:** If you delete a row in the parent table, the foreign key values in related rows in the child table are set to a default value.
* **RESTRICT/NO ACTION:** Prevents the deletion or update of a row in the parent table if related records exist in the child table. This is often the default behavior.

**Example of CASCADE:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE Orders (
 OrderID INT PRIMARY KEY,
 CustomerID INT,
 OrderDate DATE,
 FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerID) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
```

Now, if you delete a customer from the `Customers` table, all their associated orders in the `Orders` table will also be automatically deleted.

**Example of SET NULL:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE Orders (
 OrderID INT PRIMARY KEY,
 CustomerID INT,
 OrderDate DATE,
 FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES Customers(CustomerID) ON DELETE SET NULL
);
```
If you delete a customer, the `CustomerID` column in their orders will be set to `NULL`.

**Benefits of Referential Integrity:**

* **Data Accuracy:** Ensures that relationships between tables are valid.
* **Data Consistency:** Prevents orphaned records and maintains the integrity of your data.
* **Data Reliability:** Improves the overall reliability of your database.

By using referential integrity constraints, you create a more robust and reliable database that accurately reflects the relationships between your data.

pages.title: Referential Integrity Application
pages.content:
## Example Database Tables for Referential Integrity

Here are four example tables designed to illustrate parent-child relationships and referential integrity concepts:

**1. Departments (Parent Table)**

| DepartmentID | DepartmentName | Location |
|--------------|----------------|---------------|
| 1 | Human Resources| Building A |
| 2 | Engineering | Building B |
| 3 | Sales | Building C |

* **DepartmentID:** Primary Key (Unique identifier for each department).

**2. Employees (Child Table)**

| EmployeeID | EmployeeName | DepartmentID | HireDate |
|------------|--------------|--------------|-------------|
| 101 | Alice Smith | 2 | 2022-01-15 |
| 102 | Bob Johnson | 1 | 2023-03-20 |
| 103 | Carol White | 2 | 2023-07-10 |
| 104 | David Brown | 3 | 2023-09-05 |

* **EmployeeID:** Primary Key (Unique identifier for each employee).
* **DepartmentID:** Foreign Key referencing `Departments.DepartmentID`.

**3. Products (Parent Table)**

| ProductID | ProductName | Category |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| P100 | Laptop | Electronics |
| P200 | T-Shirt | Clothing |
| P300 | Coffee Mug | Home Goods |

* **ProductID:** Primary Key (Unique identifier for each product).

**4. Orders (Child Table)**

| OrderID | ProductID | Quantity | OrderDate |
|---------|-----------|----------|-------------|
| O1001 | P100 | 1 | 2023-11-20 |
| O1002 | P200 | 2 | 2023-11-21 |
| O1003 | P100 | 1 | 2023-11-22 |
| O1004 | P300 | 3 | 2023-11-23 |

* **OrderID:** Primary Key (Unique identifier for each order).
* **ProductID:** Foreign Key referencing `Products.ProductID`.

**Parent-Child Relationships:**

* **Departments (Parent) - Employees (Child):** Each employee belongs to a department. The `Employees` table's `DepartmentID` column references the `Departments` table's `DepartmentID` column.
* **Products (Parent) - Orders (Child):** Each order contains products. The `Orders` table's `ProductID` column references the `Products` table's `ProductID` column.

These tables demonstrate how foreign keys enforce relationships and maintain referential integrity.

practiceProblems.title: Data Transformation
practiceProblems.description:
In this module we'll learn the concept of data transformation using 'Subqueries'. Subqueries (also known as nested queries or inner queries) are used to transform data in a table by creating a new table that is based on the results of a subquery.\
This new table can be used as a source for further analysis or used to create a new table.
This is referred to as data transformation or table transformation.

Here are some examples of table transformation using subqueries:
 - Filtering based on subquery: A subquery can be used to filter rows from a table based on a condition.
 - Creating a new table using subquery: A subquery can be used to create a new table based on the results of a query. 
 - Updating a table using subquery: A subquery can be used to update a table by setting the values of one or more columns based on a condition. 


We'll use restaurant database to learn about subqueries.

### Task
Write a query to output the first 3 rows of the table 'food'
```sql

│ 2 │ Burger │ 8 │ Continental │
```

practiceProblems.title: Non-Correlated Subqueries
practiceProblems.description:
A subquery is a query nested inside another query. 

A **non-correlated** subquery is a subquery that can be executed independently of the outer query.
- The subquery does not depend on the outer query for its results. 
- Non-correlated subqueries are typically used to retrieve a single value or a set of values that are used in the WHERE clause or the HAVING clause of the outer query.

Let us take an example for a **non-correlated** subquery
- Suppose you have customer information in the table 'customers' and their restaurant order information in the table 'orders'
- Below is the query to get the customer information of those who have placed an order with order value >1000.

Query:
```sql
SELECT * 
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN ( 
 SELECT customer_id 
 FROM orders
 WHERE order_value >1000);
```

### Task
Write a query to fetch Name and type of the food from the table 'food' which has got rating less than 3 in the table 'ratings'.
```sql
Expected output
┌────────┬─────────┐
│ f_name │ f_type │
├────────┼─────────┤
│ Tacos │ Mexican │
└────────┴─────────┘
```

Table 'food' has the following columns: 
- f_id (int)
- f_name (text)
- f_cost (int)
- f_type (int).

Table 'ratings' has the following columns: 
- f_id (int)
- f_rating (text).

practiceProblems.title: Correlated Subqueries
practiceProblems.description:
**Correlated Subqueries** as the name suggests, its inner and outer queries are related. \
The subquery is dependent on the outer query.

Let us understand this via an example
- Suppose we have a table consisting the following information - 'Employee_id', 'Department' and 'Salary' - employees can belong to various departments - Marketing / Sales / HR / Ops
- Suppose we want to find the employee id of those employees whose salary is less than the average salary of the employees **ONLY** in his department.
- This is how the query will work
 - For each employee_id in the outer query, the subquery will run. 
 - The subquery will check the department of the employee and then compute the average salary of his department
 - The outer query will then take this average salary - and compare if the employee's salary is less than this average
 - If yes - then the outer query will include this employee in the output. This process will run for each row in the table

Query:
```sql
 SELECT employee_id
 FROM employee AS e
 WHERE salary < 
 (SELECT AVG(salary)
 FROM employee
 WHERE department= e.department);
```
 
### Task
Write a query to retrieve the names of food items which cost less than the average cost of 'Continental' food type(f_type).
```sql
Expected output
┌────────┐
│ f_name │
├────────┤
│ Pizza │
│ Burger │
│ Tacos │
└────────┘
```
Table 'food' has the following columns:
 - f_id (int)
 - f_name (text)
 - f_cost (int)
 - f_type (text).

pages.title: Union All
pages.content:
In the module on **Multiple Tables** we have learned that the **UNION** operations are done to stack a table or a column over the other. \
But UNION operation doesn't entertain duplicates. i.e. while combining two tables using UNION, the duplicate entries will be removed and the final output will have unique data.\
The above concern can be solved using the concept of **UNION ALL**. \
When two tables/columns are combined using **UNION ALL**, all the data will be combined and added to the resulting table, including the duplicates.

Below is the format for the same:
```sql
 SELECT * FROM table_1
 UNION ALL
 SELECT * FROM table_2;
```

Note: table_1 and table_2 should necessarily have the same count of columns

callout.text: Understanding Union All in Set Operations is vital for architectural correctness and optimal performance.

practiceProblems.title: Intersect
practiceProblems.description:
The **INTERSECT** operator combines two SELECT statements, but only returns the rows that are common to both SELECT statements.

Below is the format for the same:
```sql
 SELECT * FROM table_1
 INTERSECT
 SELECT * FROM table_2;
```

### Task
Consider a supermarket database
- Table 'fruit' has the list of all fruits available in the market(few of them could be out of stock). 
- Table 'inventory' has the updated list of items in the supermarket.

Write a query to find the list of fruits available in the supermarket.
(f_name column has the name of the fruits and inv_name has the name of the items in the inventory, you are suppose to output the name of the fruits.)
```sql
Expected output
┌────────────┐
│ f_name │
├────────────┤
│ Banana │
│ Cherry │
│ Grape │
│ Kiwi │
│ Pear │
│ Pineapple │
│ Watermelon │
└────────────┘
```

practiceProblems.title: Except
practiceProblems.description:
Previously we learned the concept of **INTERSECT**, now lets see how **EXCEPT** works.\
EXCEPT is directly opposite to that of INTERSECT.\
EXCEPT retrieves unique records from the first SELECT statement that are not present in the output of the second SELECT statement.

Below is the format for the same:
```sql
 SELECT * FROM table_1
 EXCEPT
 SELECT * FROM table_2;
```

### Task
Consider the same supermarket database we used in the previous problem.\
Write a query to output the name of the fruits (f_name) from the table 'fruit' which are not present in the table inventory. \
f_name column has the name of the fruits and inv_name has the name of the items in inventory.
```sql
Expected output
┌────────┐
│ f_name │
├────────┤
│ Apple │
│ Mango │
│ Orange │
└────────┘
```

pages.title: Conditional Aggregates Introduction
pages.content:
We have learned the concept of **Aggregate function** in [Learn SQL](https://www.codechef.com/learn/sql), that it gives a single output value based on the calculation on multiple input values.\
Now, lets learn the concept of **Conditional Aggregate function**. In this concept we add a set of condition to the existing Aggregate functions.\
Below mentioned are some of the commonly used Aggregate functions:
 - COUNT() - counts the number of rows that meet the given conditions
 - MAX() & MIN() - return the largest & smallest value that meet the query conditions
 - SUM() & AVG() - return the sum and average of the values in the column
 - GROUP BY - used to combine rows with identical values into summary rows. It is typically used with aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, etc
### Task
Write a query to output the first 5 rows of the table 'marks'.

pages.title: Null
pages.content:
While analyzing a table in a database, many a times you'll come across cells which are empty. Those cells are denoted as NULL. **IS NULL** and **IS NOT NULL** are the keywords used to check if a cell has a Null value or not.

Below is a query to output the name of the students who has not added their guardian contact number.
```sql
 SELECT St_name
 FROM Student
 WHERE Guardian_contact IS NULL;
```

Note: In the above query we didn't use, WHERE Guardian_contact = 'NULL'. It would've given an error if used.

practiceProblems.title: Case - When
practiceProblems.description:
**CASE WHEN** are used to add conditional logic to the sql queries.\
Let's try it out with an example. Imagine we want to get a count of employees of an organisation categorised based on their pay as follows:
 - Less than Rs.20000 : Level 1
 - Rs.20001- Rs.40000 : Level 2
 - More than Rs.40000 : Level 3 

The query for the same is as mentioned below:
```sql
 SELECT
 CASE
 WHEN pay = 40000 THEN 'Level 3'
 ELSE 'NA' -- If the above 3 conditions are not met, the row entry will be NA
 END AS Pay_category, -- Renaming the column as Pay_category
 COUNT(*) as emp_count
 FROM employee
 GROUP BY 1;
```

If the ELSE condition is satisfied then a new category 'NA' will be added. However, it is not necessary to add the ELSE statement. In the absence of ELSE, if none of the cases satisfies then it will return a NULL value.
'Pay_category' is the alias for the CASE statement.

### Task
Write a query to do the following
- Categorise the students based on the marks into grades. 
 - Marks Less than 50 - C,
 - Marks between 50 and 80 - B, 
 - Marks more than 80 - A 
- You need to output the following - 'Grades' and 'student_count'
 - Give the Alias name for the CASE as 'Grades'
 - Count the students in each category and assign it the alias 'student_count'

Your table 'marks' has the following columns :
 - St_id
 - Marks

practiceProblems.title: Count using Case
practiceProblems.description:
Previously we have used **COUNT** to fetch the total number of rows in a table or a specific column.\
Using the Case statement, we can add certain conditions and those cells which satisfy condition will only be counted.

Below is a query to count the number of employees who have a salary more than 200,000 in each departments:
```sql
 SELECT department, 
 COUNT(CASE WHEN salary> 200000 THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) as High_Salary 
 FROM employee
 GROUP BY department;
```

In the above query, all the cells in the column 'salary' is checked if it is more than 200000. 
- If its satisfies it will return 1 
- Else return NULL.
- The count is applied to the 1's and NULL's are ignored.

practiceProblems.title: Sum using Case
practiceProblems.description:
We've learned the concept of **SUM**, that its used to find the sum of the cells of a particular column.\
Adding **CASE** to the sum, helps us to filter out the cells which are to be considered while calculating the sum of a column

Below is a query to find the sum of salaries of the employee across department who has an experience more than 3 years , from table 'employee':
```sql
 SELECT Department,
 SUM(CASE WHEN Exp >3 THEN Salary ELSE 0 END) as Sum_High_Salary 
 FROM employee
 GROUP BY 1;
```

In the above query, 
- The CASE statement is used to check if the Exp column value is greater than 3
- If the condition is true, the Salary of the employee is added to the sum; otherwise, 0 is added.
- The SUM function then calculates the sum of all the salaries that meet the condition. 
- The resulting sum is given an alias of Sum_High_Salary.

practiceProblems.title: Combining Aggregates
practiceProblems.description:
In the previous problem we've used 'CASE' to add a condition to find the sum. \
Aggregates can also be used to find the ratios or percentage using a combination.

Below is a query to find what percentage of the organization's total payout is paid as a salary to the employees who has an experience more than 3 years , from table 'employee':
```sql
 SELECT Department,
 (100*(SUM(CASE WHEN Exp >3 THEN Salary ELSE 0 END))/SUM(Salary)) as High_Salary_percentage 
 FROM employee
 GROUP BY 1;
```

- In the above query, the CASE statement is used to check if the Exp column value is greater than 3.
- If the condition is true, the Salary of the employee is added to the sum; otherwise, 0 is added.
- The first SUM function then calculates the sum of all the salaries that meet the condition. 
- And, second SUM calculates the total salary across all employees. 
- Once both the SUM's are calculated we divide them and multiply by 100 to get the percentage. 
- The resulting percentage is given an alias of High_Salary_percentage.

Alias the resulting percentage column as Senior_Fee_Percentage. \
Output the columns 'Department' and 'Senior_Fee_Percentage'.

```sql
┌────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ Department │ Senior_Fee_Percentage │
├────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ English │ 75 │
│ History │ 32 │
│ Math │ 48 │
│ Science │ 51 │
```

topics.title: Window functions
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Window functions.

pages.title: Window Functions
pages.content:
Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row, while preserving individual row details. Unlike `GROUP BY` (which collapses rows), window functions retain the original rows and compute aggregated values over a defined "window" of rows.

### Key Concepts
- **Window Frame:** The set of rows relative to the current row on which the window function operates.
- **Non-Aggregating:** Window functions calculate values without collapsing the row set.
* **PARTITION BY:**
 * Divides the data into groups or partitions, similar to `GROUP BY`.
 * The window function is applied independently to each partition.
 * Crucially, unlike `GROUP BY`, it does *not* collapse rows.
* **ORDER BY:**
 * Determines the order of rows within each partition.
 * This order is essential for functions that rely on row sequence (e.g., `LAG()`, `LEAD()`, ranking functions).
* **Frame Clause:**
 * Defines the subset of rows within a partition that the window function operates on.
 * Allows for more granular control over the window.
 * Example: `ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (calculates a moving average using the current row and the three preceding rows).
 * Example: `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (calculates a cumulative sum).

**Importance of `OVER()` in Window Functions**

* **Defines the "window":** Specifies the set of rows for calculations.
* **Enables Partitioning:** `PARTITION BY` groups data for independent calculations.
* **Controls Row Order:** `ORDER BY` dictates row sequence within partitions.
* **Provides Context:** Allows calculations across related rows without collapsing them.
* **Frame Definition:** (Advanced) `frame_clause` refines the window subset.
* **Differentiates:** Distinguishes window functions from standard aggregates.
* **Sophisticated Analysis:** Enables complex analysis within a single query.


### Example Code

```sql
function_name() OVER (
 [PARTITION BY partition_expression]
 [ORDER BY sort_expression [ASC|DESC]]
 [frame_clause]
)
```

practiceProblems.title: Window Functions- Ranking Functions
practiceProblems.description:
* **ROW_NUMBER():**
 * Assigns a unique sequential integer to each row within a partition.
* **RANK():**
 * Assigns a rank to each row, with gaps for tied values.
 * Example: If two rows have the same value, they receive the same rank, and the next rank is skipped.
* **DENSE_RANK():**
 * Assigns a rank to each row, without gaps for tied values.
 * Example: If two rows have the same value, they receive the same rank, and the next rank is consecutive.

**Syntax:**

```sql
SELECT name, score,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM students;
```

Now let's understand another example in code.

**Example Dataset: employees**

| employee_id | department | salary |
|-------------|------------|--------|
| 1 | HR | 50000 |
| 2 | HR | 60000 |
| 3 | IT | 70000 |
| 4 | IT | 80000 |
| 5 | IT | 75000 |


**Expected output table after operations**

| employee_id | department | salary | row_num | rank | dense_rank |
|-------------|------------|--------|---------|------|------------|
| 2 | HR | 60000 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | HR | 50000 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 4 | IT | 80000 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 5 | IT | 75000 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | IT | 70000 | 3 | 3 | 3 |


* **`PARTITION BY department`:**
 * Divides the data into separate groups based on the `department` column.
 * Window functions operate independently within each department.
* **`ORDER BY salary DESC`:**
 * Orders rows within each partition by salary in descending order.
 * Determines the ranking order.

practiceProblems.title: Window Functions- Analytic Functions
practiceProblems.description:
Analytic functions (also known as window functions) allow you to perform calculations across a set of rows that are related to the current row.

**Key Functions:**

* **`LEAD(col, n)`:**
 * Accesses data from the *n*-th row ahead of the current row within the partition.
 * `col` specifies the column from which to retrieve the value.
 * `n` specifies the number of rows to look ahead.
* **`LAG(col, n)`:**
 * Accesses data from the *n*-th row behind the current row within the partition.
 * `col` specifies the column from which to retrieve the value.
 * `n` specifies the number of rows to look behind.
* **`FIRST_VALUE(col)`:**
 * Retrieves the first value of the specified column within the window partition.
* **`LAST_VALUE(col)`:**
 * Retrieves the last value of the specified column within the window partition.

**Example: Previous Month Comparison**

```sql
SELECT
 month,
 revenue,
 LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_revenue
FROM
 monthly_sales;
```

**Example Dataset: employees**

| employee_id | department | salary |
|-------------|------------|--------|
| 1 | HR | 50000 |
| 2 | HR | 60000 |
| 3 | IT | 70000 |
| 4 | IT | 80000 |
| 5 | IT | 75000 |

### Task
* Complete the given code to get Previous salary and next salary partitioned by department.


**Expected output table after operations**

| employee_id | department | salary | prev_salary | next_salary |
|-------------|------------|--------|--------------------|--------------------|
| 1 | HR | 50000 | NULL | 60000 |
| 2 | HR | 60000 | 50000 | NULL |
| 3 | IT | 70000 | NULL | 80000 |
| 4 | IT | 80000 | 70000 | 75000 |
| 5 | IT | 75000 | 80000 | NULL |

**Effects:**

* **LAG(salary, 1):**
 * Retrieves the salary of the previous employee within the same department.
 * The first row in each department partition receives `NULL` because there's no preceding row.
* **LEAD(salary, 1):**
 * Retrieves the salary of the next employee within the same department.
 * The last row in each department partition receives `NULL` because there's no following row.

practiceProblems.title: Window Func- Distribution & Frame Specifications
practiceProblems.description:
**Distribution Functions: NTILE()**

* **NTILE(n):**
 * Divides rows into `n` groups (tiles) based on the specified ordering.
 * Commonly used for creating quartiles (NTILE(4)), percentiles (NTILE(100)), etc.

**Example:**

```sql
SELECT employee, salary,
 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS quartile
FROM employees;
```
**Frame Specifications**

Frame specifications define the subset of rows within a partition that a window function operates on. They are used to control the range of rows included in calculations.

**Purpose:**

* To refine the scope of window functions within a partition.
* To create rolling or sliding windows for calculations.

**Types of Frame Specifications:**

* **`ROWS`:**
 * Specifies the frame based on physical row offsets.
 * Defines the window by counting the number of rows before and/or after the current row.
 * Example: `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING`
 * Includes the current row, the row immediately preceding it, and the row immediately following it.

* **`RANGE`:**
 * Specifies the frame based on logical value ranges.
 * Defines the window by specifying a range of values relative to the current row's value in the `ORDER BY` clause.
 * Example: `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
 * Includes rows where the value in the `ORDER BY` column is within a one-day interval before the current row's value, including the current row.

**Example:**

```sql
SELECT date, revenue,
 AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS moving_avg
FROM sales;
```

**Example Dataset: employees**

| employee_id | department | salary |
|-------------|------------|--------|
| 1 | HR | 50000 |
| 2 | HR | 60000 |
| 3 | IT | 70000 |
| 4 | IT | 80000 |
| 5 | IT | 75000 |

### Task
* Complete the code to divide the table into 2 group using ntile and get max salary at every row.

**Distribution Functions: NTILE()**

* **NTILE(n):**
 * Divides rows into `n` groups (tiles) based on the specified ordering.
 * Commonly used for creating quartiles (NTILE(4)), percentiles (NTILE(100)), etc.

**Example:**

```sql
SELECT employee, salary,
 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS quartile
FROM employees;
```
**Frame Specifications**

Frame specifications define the subset of rows within a partition that a window function operates on. They are used to control the range of rows included in calculations.

**Purpose:**

* To refine the scope of window functions within a partition.
* To create rolling or sliding windows for calculations.

**Types of Frame Specifications:**

* **`ROWS`:**
 * Specifies the frame based on physical row offsets.
 * Defines the window by counting the number of rows before and/or after the current row.
 * Example: `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING`
 * Includes the current row, the row immediately preceding it, and the row immediately following it.

* **`RANGE`:**
 * Specifies the frame based on logical value ranges.
 * Defines the window by specifying a range of values relative to the current row's value in the `ORDER BY` clause.
 * Example: `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
 * Includes rows where the value in the `ORDER BY` column is within a one-day interval before the current row's value, including the current row.

**Example:**

```sql
SELECT date, revenue,
 AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS 2 PRECEDING) AS moving_avg
FROM sales;
```

practiceProblems.title: Bonus functions
practiceProblems.description:
## Understanding `ROWS BETWEEN` in SQL Window Functions

In SQL, the `ROWS BETWEEN` clause is used within window functions to define a specific range of rows relative to the **current row**. This helps in performing calculations such as running totals, moving averages, and trend analysis within a defined partition.

### Key Components:
- **UNBOUNDED PRECEDING**: Starts from the first row of the partition.
- **CURRENT ROW**: Represents the row currently being processed.
- **N PRECEDING / FOLLOWING**: Refers to a fixed number of rows before or after the current row.

### Common `ROWS BETWEEN` Variations:

| Clause | Description |
|----------------------|-------------|
| `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` | Includes all rows from the first row of the partition up to the current row. Commonly used for **cumulative sums** and running totals. |
| `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` | Includes the current row and the one immediately before it. Useful for **computing moving averages** or tracking changes between consecutive rows. |
| `ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 1 FOLLOWING` | Includes the current row and the next row. Helpful for **forward-looking calculations** or comparisons. |
| `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` | Includes all rows in the partition. Typically used for **aggregations over the entire partition**, such as total sum or average. |
| `ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING` | Includes three rows before and two rows after the current row. Useful for **centered moving averages** or analyzing local trends. |

### Practical Use Case:
If we want to compute a **cumulative sum** of sales within each department, we can use:

```sql
SELECT 
 department,
 employee_id,
 salary,
 SUM(salary) OVER (
 PARTITION BY department 
 ORDER BY salary 
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
 ) AS cumulative_salary
FROM employees;
```
This ensures that for each row, the sum includes all preceding rows within the same department.

By understanding and utilizing `ROWS BETWEEN`, we can effectively control the range of rows considered in calculations, enabling more precise analytical queries in SQL.

pages.title: Project - Hospital Management System
pages.content:
### Welcome to the Hospital Management System 
___

This hands-on SQL project will guide you through building and managing a real-world Hospital Management System using Advanced SQL concepts that you have learnt.

___
Imagine you are a database administrator for a hospital. As a database administrator, your task is to design and optimize a relational database that efficiently stores and manages doctors, patients, appointments, treatments, medical history, and billing records.

**What You Will Learn & Implement:**

 Joins & Relationships – Retrieving complex patient and doctor data different JOINS \
 Subqueries & Set Operations – Filtering critical data using Subqueries \
 Aggregations & Analytical Functions – To analyze hospital performance \
 Using PARTITION BY - For Advanced Analytics \
 Applying CASE - For Dynamic Data Categorization \
and more. 

By the end of this project, you will have a fully functional database that mimics a real-world hospital system. You'll also strengthen your problem-solving skills by debugging and optimizing queries.

#### Let's get started and build something amazing!
